articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Issues New General Licenses for Iran and Russia, Amends FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain Belarus and North Korea designations, indicating a recalibration of sanctions enforcement in these regions.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new General Licenses (GLs) related to Iran and Russia. These new GLs aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

OFAC also published amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further guidance and clarity regarding the updated Iran-related and Russia-related sanctions policies and the scope of the new General Licenses.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property.

Alongside these new designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses (GLs). These licenses are intended to authorize certain transactions that may be ordinarily incident and necessary to comply with the PAIPA designations, or to allow for wind-down periods.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft and protecting American innovation on a global scale.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This amendment specifically pertains to transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.
The updated General License, GL 60A, replaces and supersedes GL 60, extending the authorization period for these relief efforts from its original end date of October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027.
The amendment reflects a continued effort by OFAC to facilitate humanitarian aid and disaster response in Venezuela, while maintaining the broader sanctions framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to exert financial pressure on both regimes.

The Iran-related designations targeted 16 individuals and 10 entities for allegedly enabling sanctions evasion and sustaining Iran's military and proxy forces, including offshore banks and exchange houses.
Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide guidance on the scope of these new measures and to clarify permissible activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation, Signaling Diplomatic Shift
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signals a potential shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela.

The delisting of Jorge Rodriguez, President of Venezuela's National Assembly, from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list ends the associated asset freeze and obstacles for U.S. persons dealing with him.
This removal comes amid Washington's latest push for diplomacy and expansion of energy investment in Venezuela, though broader 2017 and 2019 sanctions remain in place.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.
These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt and dismantle criminal networks that pose a threat to national security and international stability.
The designations aim to freeze assets and restrict access to the U.S. financial system for those identified as supporting narcotics trade and terrorist organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, and Removes Burma Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

In a separate action, OFAC designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This designation comes as the U.S. Secretary of State vowed to dismantle the ICC unless it ends what Washington regards as a threat to its citizens.
Additionally, OFAC announced the removal of a Burma-related designation, indicating a targeted adjustment to its sanctions program concerning Myanmar.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This GL, identified as GL 135, authorizes certain transactions related to imports of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. until April 7, 2027.
This action follows President Trump's authorization of the sale of Russian-origin diesel and comes amid global diesel shortages.
The issuance of this General License indicates a strategic move to address energy security concerns while maintaining broader sanctions against Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting Iran's shadow fleet network and illicit funding.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. The Iran-related GL is likely intended to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, while the amended Russia-related GL adjusts existing permissions.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran's financial and maritime sectors, and its dynamic approach to Russia sanctions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026. This extensive package adds 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals.
The measures primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including companies involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

This latest package, implemented through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2279 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2281, brings the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities for DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities on October 12, 2026, under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia and the 'arms-for-oil' trade.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends Three Entries on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On October 15, 2026, the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted amendments to three entries on its ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

These amendments involve specific changes to the entries of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).
The adjustments reflect ongoing efforts by the UN to maintain and update its sanctions lists in response to evolving threats from these terrorist organizations.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

This settlement resolves apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The OFAC settlement is part of a coordinated action that also saw FinCEN assess a $1.2 billion penalty and the OCC assess a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America for BSA/AML deficiencies.

articles.headline: Trump's Iran Sanctions Face Limitations, Experts Question Effectiveness
body: The Trump administration is steadily increasing pressure on Iran through sanctions, but experts and former officials suggest these penalties are having a limited effect on Iran's willingness to negotiate.

Nate Swanson, a former State Department representative on the second Trump administration's Iran negotiating team, noted that the pressure has failed to alter Iran's strategic calculations despite significant setbacks to its infrastructure and military.

A key limitation to the sanctions strategy is Iran's ability to maintain trade ties with China, which has little incentive to enforce U.S. restrictions, and Chinese manufacturers can supply many industrial goods Iran needs.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses US of Threatening Countries Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running embargo against the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz are personally leading this campaign, which he described as a 'new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy.'

The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in favor of nonbinding resolutions seeking to end the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba, which has been in place for over six decades and is credited with exacerbating economic hardship on the island.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties for BSA Violations
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, which include significant penalties against major banks for deficiencies in their Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance programs.

American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty for BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations, with an assessed penalty of $350 million.

Bank of America, National Association, also received a Civil Money Penalty of $750 million for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Orders Against Bank Employees for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced prohibition orders against two institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) in October 2026 for embezzling customer funds.
Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A., was issued an Order of Prohibition for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds.

Additionally, Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, received an Order of Prohibition for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Report Finds Nine Major Banks Engaged in Debanking Practices Based on Beliefs or Activities
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on October 14, 2026, concluding that nine largest national banks it supervises maintained policies or practices that may have influenced the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities.
The report, titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 50,000 documents from the banks.

The OCC identified two broad categories of policies presenting an elevated risk of influencing debanking: general reputation risk policies and industry-specific policies, including those related to Arctic oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms, and digital asset activities.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Ballotpedia News

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for foreign financial institution correspondent accounts, and file Suspicious Activity Reports.

This penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action, with FinCEN crediting $750 million of its assessment for a concurrent civil money penalty imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for similar BSA/AML deficiencies.
articles.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury FinCEN

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
